name: Routes past a drop point
brief:
A picking robot crosses a warehouse floor from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, one step right or one step down at a time. The floor is `grid`, a list of equal-length strings: `#` is a shelf the robot cannot enter, `.` is open floor and `P` is a drop point.

Write `drop_point_routes(grid)`, which returns how many routes pass through at least one drop point, modulo 1,000,000,007. The start and end cells are part of every route.

Example. For the rows `..P`, `.#.` and `...`, two routes get past the shelf. Only the one along the top row meets the drop point, so the answer is 1.
constraints: At most $80$ rows and $80$ columns, all rows the same length. The top-left and bottom-right cells are never `#`.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Adding up the routes through each `P` counts a route twice when it meets two of them. Count every route, then the routes that meet no `P`, and subtract.

examples.note: The route down the left side meets no drop point; the one along the top does.
The start cell is a drop point, so all 3 routes count.
Two routes pass both drop points and are counted once each.

tests.call: drop_point_routes([''.join('#' if (i * 7 + j * 13) % 11 == 0 and 0 < i + j < 158 else 'P' if (i * 3 + j * 5) % 97 == 1 else '.' for j in range(80)) for i in range(80)])

how: Submit runs 15 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. Unlike a plain count of routes past shelves, the drop points need a second count, because one route can meet several of them.
notes: The routes through a drop point are all the routes less the routes that meet none.
A `P` cell passes nothing on to the count of routes that meet no drop point, and that includes the start cell.
Each cell is filled once from two neighbours, so the work is $O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$.

planted.slip: Adding up the routes through each drop point counts a route once for every drop point it meets.
Starting both counts at 1 forgets that the start cell itself may be a drop point.
Leaving out the modulus returns the full count, which on a large floor runs to dozens of digits.
Reducing both counts but not their difference returns a negative number when the first residue is the smaller.
